title: Histograms
summary: A [[histogram|histogram]] shows grouped data as touching bars, where the area of each bar shows how many values are in its class. The height of a bar is its [[frequency-density|frequency density]]: the frequency divided by the class width. This stops a wide class looking bigger than it really is.

goals.text: Work out the frequency density of each class in a [[grouped-frequency-table|grouped frequency table]].
Draw a histogram for classes of different widths.
Read frequencies from a histogram, including an estimate for part of a class.
Find bar heights or a missing frequency when heights are given in centimetres or a bar is missing.

before.prompt: A class in a grouped frequency table is $35 < h \le 50$. What is its class width?
before.hint: Subtract the lower boundary from the upper boundary.
before.explain: Class width $=$ upper boundary $-$ lower boundary $= 50 - 35 = 15$. Revise it in {{lesson:9.3}}.

before.prompt: A grouped frequency table has the classes $10 < t \le 20$ and $20 < t \le 30$. Is a time of exactly $20$ in the class $20 < t \le 30$?
before.hint: Read $20 < t$ as "$t$ is more than $20$".

options.text: No, it goes in the class below

before.explain: $20 < t$ means $t$ is more than $20$, so $20$ itself is not in this class. It belongs to $10 < t \le 20$, since $t \le 20$ includes $20$. Revise it in {{lesson:9.3}}.

verify.truth: No, it goes in the class below

sections.heading: Frequency density and drawing a histogram

blocks.text: A [[grouped-frequency-table|grouped frequency table]] can have [[class-interval|class intervals]] of different widths. Then a bar chart of the frequencies misleads you.

Say $12$ people wait between $0$ and $5$ minutes, and $12$ wait between $5$ and $30$ minutes. The first $12$ are packed into $5$ minutes. The second $12$ are spread over $25$ minutes. A fair picture makes the first bar taller.

blocks.statement: The [[frequency-density|frequency density]] of a class is its frequency divided by its class width.
blocks.plain: How many values there are for each unit of width.

blocks.statement: A [[histogram|histogram]] shows grouped data as touching bars whose areas are proportional to the frequencies. When each height is the frequency density, the area of each bar equals its frequency.
blocks.plain: Area, not height, shows how many values are in a class.

blocks.text: Why does dividing by the width work? Area $=$ width $\times$ height $=$ class width $\times \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}} =$ frequency.

blocks.question: The table shows how long some students spent on homework one evening. $\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{Time } (t \text{ minutes}) & 0 < t \le 10 & 10 < t \le 15 & 15 < t \le 45 & 45 < t \le 90 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 7 & 14 & 33 & 36 \end{array}$ Work out the frequency density of each class. Which class has the tallest bar on a histogram?
steps: Find each class width, upper boundary minus lower: $10 - 0 = 10$, $15 - 10 = 5$, $45 - 15 = 30$ and $90 - 45 = 45$.
Divide each frequency by its width: $7 \div 10 = 0.7$, $14 \div 5 = 2.8$, $33 \div 30 = 1.1$ and $36 \div 45 = 0.8$.
The largest frequency density is $2.8$, so the $10 < t \le 15$ bar is the tallest.
The class $45 < t \le 90$ has the most students, $36$. But they are spread over $45$ minutes, so its bar is low.

blocks.text: 1. Work out each class width and frequency density. Two extra columns in the table keep this tidy.
2. Draw a continuous scale for the data along the horizontal axis. Label the vertical axis "Frequency density".
3. Draw each bar from its lower class boundary to its upper one, as tall as its frequency density. The bars touch, with no gaps.

blocks.question: The table shows the heights of $36$ seedlings. $\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{Height } (h \text{ cm}) & 0 < h \le 4 & 4 < h \le 6 & 6 < h \le 7 & 7 < h \le 10 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 6 & 13 & 8 & 9 \end{array}$ Draw a histogram to show this information.
steps: Frequency densities: $6 \div 4 = 1.5$, $13 \div 2 = 6.5$, $8 \div 1 = 8$ and $9 \div 3 = 3$.
The tallest bar is $8$, so run the vertical axis from $0$ to $8$. Label it "Frequency density".
Draw four touching bars: $0$ to $4$ at height $1.5$, $4$ to $6$ at $6.5$, $6$ to $7$ at $8$, and $7$ to $10$ at $3$.
Check one bar by its area: $6.5 \times 2 = 13$, the frequency in the table.

blocks.alt: Histogram of seedling heights. Height in cm across, from 0 to 10. Frequency density up, from 0 to 8, with each small square 0.5. Four touching bars: 0 to 4 cm at height 1.5, 4 to 6 cm at height 6.5, 6 to 7 cm at height 8, and 7 to 10 cm at height 3.
blocks.caption: The $6 < h \le 7$ bar is the tallest, though its class holds only $8$ seedlings.

blocks.text: Don't use the frequency as the height. With unequal widths, that makes wide classes look too big. Divide by the class width first.

blocks.prompt: A class $15 < m \le 40$ has frequency $35$. Work out its frequency density.
blocks.hint: Find the class width first: upper boundary minus lower boundary.

blocks.prompt: A table has classes $0 < x \le 6$, $6 < x \le 21$ and $21 < x \le 28$, with frequencies $15$, $33$ and $14$. How tall is the tallest bar on its histogram?
blocks.hint: Work out all three frequency densities, then compare them.
blocks.explain: The frequency densities are $15 \div 6 = 2.5$, $33 \div 15 = 2.2$ and $14 \div 7 = 2$, so the tallest bar is $2.5$. $33$ is a frequency, not a height. $2.2$ is the bar of the class with the most values.

blocks.text: Reading a histogram reverses the drawing. The area of a bar is the frequency of its class.
Before you read any heights, work out what one small square on each axis is worth.

blocks.alt: Histogram of apple masses. Mass in grams across, from 100 to 200. Frequency density up, from 0 to 3.5, with each small square 0.1. Four touching bars: 100 to 120 g at height 0.8, 120 to 130 g at height 3.2, 130 to 150 g at height 2.1, and 150 to 200 g at height 0.4.
blocks.caption: The masses of the apples picked from one tree.

blocks.question: The histogram shows the masses, $m$ grams, of the apples picked from one tree. Work out how many apples were picked.
steps: Each small square up is $0.1$. Read the heights: $0.8$, $3.2$, $2.1$ and $0.4$.
Multiply each height by its class width: $0.8 \times 20 = 16$, $3.2 \times 10 = 32$, $2.1 \times 20 = 42$ and $0.4 \times 50 = 20$.
Add the frequencies: $16 + 32 + 42 + 20 = 110$.

blocks.text: For part of a class, assume its values are spread evenly across the class. Then use the width of just that part. The answer is an estimate.

blocks.question: Use the same histogram. Calculate an estimate of the number of apples with a mass of more than $140$ g.
steps: Only part of the class $130 < m \le 150$ is above $140$. Assume its apples are spread evenly across the class.
The part from $140$ to $150$ has width $150 - 140 = 10$ and height $2.1$. That gives $2.1 \times 10 = 21$ apples.
All of the class $150 < m \le 200$ is above $140$: $0.4 \times 50 = 20$ apples.
Add: $21 + 20 = 41$. This is only an estimate, because you don't know where the apples lie inside a class.

blocks.text: Don't read the height of a bar as its frequency. Multiply the height by the class width.

blocks.prompt: A histogram bar goes from $25$ to $45$ on the horizontal axis. Its height is $1.8$. How many values are in its class?
blocks.hint: The frequency is the area of the bar.

blocks.prompt: A histogram bar for $10 < x \le 30$ has height $2.5$. Estimate how many values lie between $10$ and $16$.
blocks.hint: Use only the part of the bar from $10$ to $16$.
blocks.explain: The part from $10$ to $16$ has width $6$, so the estimate is $2.5 \times 6 = 15$. $50$ is the whole bar. $40$ multiplies by $16$ instead of the width.

sections.heading: Heights in centimetres and missing bars

blocks.text: Some questions give bar heights in centimetres, not on a frequency density scale. The heights are still in proportion to the frequency densities.
1. Use the bar you know. Centimetres for $1$ unit of frequency density $=$ its height $\div$ its frequency density.
2. Work out the frequency density of each other class.
3. Multiply each frequency density by the centimetres for $1$ unit.

blocks.question: The table shows how long some people waited for a bus. $\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{Time } (t \text{ minutes}) & 0 < t \le 4 & 4 < t \le 10 & 10 < t \le 12 & 12 < t \le 16 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 14 & 33 & 13 & 9 \end{array}$ On a histogram, the bar for $0 < t \le 4$ is $4.2$ cm tall. Calculate the heights, in cm, of the other three bars.
steps: Known bar: width $4$, so frequency density $= 14 \div 4 = 3.5$. It is drawn $4.2$ cm tall.
So $1$ unit of frequency density is $4.2 \div 3.5 = 1.2$ cm.
The other frequency densities: $33 \div 6 = 5.5$, $13 \div 2 = 6.5$ and $9 \div 4 = 2.25$.
Heights: $5.5 \times 1.2 = 6.6$ cm, $6.5 \times 1.2 = 7.8$ cm and $2.25 \times 1.2 = 2.7$ cm.

blocks.text: If a bar is missing but you know the total frequency, find the other frequencies first. What is left belongs to the missing class.

blocks.question: A histogram shows the distances, $d$ km, that $60$ people cycled in a week. It has bars for $0 < d \le 6$ with height $1.5$, $6 < d \le 14$ with height $2.25$, and $17 < d \le 33$ with height $0.75$. The bar for $14 < d \le 17$ is missing. Work out its height.
steps: Frequencies of the drawn bars: $1.5 \times 6 = 9$, $2.25 \times 8 = 18$ and $0.75 \times 16 = 12$.
These add to $9 + 18 + 12 = 39$, so the missing class holds $60 - 39 = 21$ people.
Its width is $17 - 14 = 3$, so its frequency density is $21 \div 3 = 7$.
Draw the bar from $14$ to $17$ at height $7$, touching the bars on each side.

blocks.text: Don't scale the heights by frequency alone. Two classes with the same frequency but different widths need different heights.

blocks.prompt: On a histogram, the class $0 < x \le 15$ has frequency $9$ and its bar is $4.8$ cm tall. The class $15 < x \le 20$ has frequency $7$. How tall is its bar, in cm?
blocks.hint: Find how many centimetres stand for $1$ unit of frequency density.
blocks.explain: First bar: frequency density $9 \div 15 = 0.6$, drawn $4.8$ cm, so $1$ unit is $4.8 \div 0.6 = 8$ cm. Second bar: $7 \div 5 = 1.4$, so its height is $1.4 \times 8 = 11.2$ cm.

blocks.prompt: On a histogram, a bar $4$ units wide is $9$ cm tall and stands for $24$ values. Another bar is $7$ units wide and $6$ cm tall. How many values does it stand for?
blocks.hint: Find the frequency density of the first bar, then the centimetres for $1$ unit.
blocks.explain: First bar: frequency density $24 \div 4 = 6$, drawn $9$ cm, so $1$ unit is $9 \div 6 = 1.5$ cm. Second bar: $6 \div 1.5 = 4$, so it stands for $4 \times 7 = 28$ values. $16$ ignores the widths, and $42$ treats centimetres as frequency density.

blocks.text: A histogram's bars touch, the horizontal axis is a continuous scale and the vertical axis is labelled "Frequency density". The area of a bar shows its frequency.
Part of a class: assume the values are spread evenly, so use height $\times$ width of that part. The answer is an estimate.
Heights in cm: cm for $1$ unit $=$ known height $\div$ its frequency density. Multiply each frequency density by it.

mistakes: Drawing each bar with the frequency as its height. Divide each frequency by its class width first, so wide classes don't look too big.
Reading a bar's height as its frequency. The frequency is the area: height $\times$ class width.
Scaling bar heights in centimetres by the frequencies. Scale by the frequency densities, because the class widths differ.
examTips: When you complete a table or draw a histogram, write each frequency density, such as $13 \div 2 = 6.5$. Correct frequency densities can still earn marks if a bar is drawn wrongly.
"Calculate an estimate" for part of a class needs the width of that part times the bar's height, such as $2.1 \times 10$. Show that product.
When heights are in centimetres, first work out the centimetres for 1 unit of frequency density from the bar you know. Show that step, as it is usually worth a method mark.
After you read frequencies from a histogram, check that they add to any total the question gives.
